questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Before standardisation, cargo was loaded piece by piece and a ship could sit at a wharf for a week. The shipping container changed less about the box than about everything around it: cranes, chassis, railway wagons and hulls were all rebuilt to one set of dimensions. Its power lay in being _____ rather than in any property of the steel it was made from.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Economists long assumed that a fishery open to everyone would be stripped bare. The lobstering harbours of the Maine coast are a standing exception: the gang working out of each harbour settles who may set traps in its waters, how many and where, and enforces those limits itself. Access to the ground is neither free nor state-controlled but _____ by the fishermen who work it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Periodical cicadas spend either thirteen or seventeen years underground and then emerge all at once. Both numbers are prime, so a predator whose own population peaks every two, three or four years can almost never have its own peak _____ with an emergence. Broods that shared a cycle with their predators were eaten out long ago.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The quilts made at Gee's Bend were pieced from worn work clothes and feed sacks, and their makers had no use for the repeating block patterns sold in catalogues. Strips run off at an angle; a colour stops where the cloth ran out. What looks _____ is in fact the outcome of choices made stitch by stitch with whatever material was to hand.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “relief” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The survey party mapped the valley floor in a fortnight, but the plateau above it took a month. On flat ground a single reading serves for a wide area; where the <u>relief</u> is broken the instrument has to be moved every few hundred metres, and each new station has to be tied back to the last.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The easing of pain or distress.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Assistance given to people in need.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Variation in the height of a land surface.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A design carved so that it projects from a flat background.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The steel pan began with oil drums left on the wharves of Trinidad after the Second World War. Players noticed that a dented drumhead sounded more than one note, and set about placing the dents on purpose, sinking the head into a shallow bowl and hammering out a facet for each pitch. Tuning a pan still means striking, listening and striking again; the note is shaped rather than fitted.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To argue that the steel pan deserves a place in the orchestral repertoire.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To compare the steel pan with other percussion instruments of the Caribbean.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To explain why oil drums were abundant in Trinidad after the war.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To describe how an instrument was developed out of salvaged material and how it is made.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The sagas say that Norse sailors carried a sunstone that showed where the sun stood on an overcast day. Crystals of Iceland spar split light into two beams whose relative brightness depends on how the sky above is polarised. <u>Turning the crystal until the two beams match identifies the plane of polarisation, and that plane points back towards the sun.</u> A crystal of just this kind was lifted from an Elizabethan wreck in the Channel in 2013.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It questions whether the sagas can be trusted on the matter.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It describes the circumstances in which a crystal was recovered from a wreck.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It compares Iceland spar with other crystals available to Norse sailors.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It explains the physical principle by which the described object would work.

questions.stem: According to the text, why did grain output hold up after the steepest slopes were retired?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Wind-blown silt lies hundreds of metres deep across the Loess Plateau, and it is fertile, soft and easily washed away; the Yellow River takes both its name and its colour from it. From 1999 farmers on the plateau were paid to stop cultivating the steepest slopes and to plant them instead. Grain output did not fall, because the terraced ground lower down now held the water that had previously run off it, and the sediment reaching the river dropped by more than half.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Sediment removed from the river was returned to the fields as fertiliser.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Farmers were compensated in grain for the land they took out of cultivation.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The terraced land lower down retained water that had previously run off, making up for the lost slopes.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The steepest slopes had never produced much grain in the first place.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Embossed alphabets for blind readers already existed when Louis Braille was a student. They used raised versions of ordinary letters, which a sighted teacher could read at a glance. Braille's system does not resemble the alphabet at all. Each cell is small enough to sit under a fingertip without the finger having to travel across it, and, unlike raised letters, it can be written by a blind person as readily as it can be read. Schools resisted it for decades.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Braille's system was designed around the reader's finger and hand rather than the sighted teacher's eye.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Raised-letter alphabets were invented only after Braille's system had appeared.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Blind readers before Braille had no means of reading at all.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Braille's system was adopted quickly because teachers found it easy to learn.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hartmann's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Asked to estimate a quantity they cannot look up, people are pulled towards any number they have just been shown, even one they know to be irrelevant. Psychologist Nils Hartmann argues that the effect is not simply a matter of inattention.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Participants took longer to answer when the number they had been shown was wildly implausible.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Experts estimating quantities in their own field are pulled towards the number less than novices are.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Participants who were warned about the effect beforehand and paid a bonus for accuracy were pulled towards the number just as strongly as those who were not.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Participants shown a larger number gave larger estimates than participants shown a smaller one.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Bakker's claim?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Draining a lake behind a dyke meant lifting water higher than any single mill could raise it. Historian Joost Bakker maintains that the decisive innovation in the great Dutch reclamations of the seventeenth century was organisational — the joint-stock company that financed and coordinated the work — rather than mechanical.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Peat cutting had enlarged many of the lakes that were later drained.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Mills capable of the necessary lift had been in use for a century before the large reclamations began, and no lake of that size was drained until the companies were formed.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The mills built for the reclamations turned to face the wind on a movable cap.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Reclaimed land sold for several times what it had cost to drain it.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Virtanen's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The upper edge of the forest on several Scandinavian mountainsides has climbed tens of metres since 1950, and birch now grows on ground that was open fell within living memory. Summers in the region have warmed over the same period, and the sheep and cattle that were driven up to the high pastures each June have almost all gone. Ecologist Sanna Virtanen argues that the cause of the shift is the ending of that grazing rather than the warming.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Summer temperatures across the region have risen by roughly one degree since 1950.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Seedlings above the present treeline survive better in warm years than in cold ones.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Grazing animals eat tree seedlings as readily as they eat grass.

choices.label: D
choices.content: On slopes where summer grazing continued at the same intensity throughout, the treeline did not move despite the same rise in temperature.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Plant matter that fell on the Siberian tundra thousands of years ago did not rot. It froze before the soil organisms could break it down and has been locked in the ground ever since. Those organisms are still present, and they resume feeding as soon as the soil thaws. Where the permafrost thaws, then, the carbon held in that ancient material _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: is taken up by the plants growing above it.

choices.label: B
choices.content: sinks below the depth at which soil organisms live.

choices.label: C
choices.content: remains fixed in the soil indefinitely.

choices.label: D
choices.content: begins to be released as the organisms resume feeding on it.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Saffron is the dried stigma of a crocus, three to a flower, and the flowers open for a few days in autumn and have to be picked at dawn before the sun opens them fully. No machine has been built that can take the stigmas out. That the spice is still the most expensive in the world by weight is therefore largely a matter of _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: the hand labour that each gram of it requires.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the difficulty of storing the dried stigmas.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the demand for it in a handful of cuisines.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the small area of land on which the crocus will grow.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A reindeer herd moves between coastal summer pasture and inland winter grazing, and the route matters more than the acreage. Because a fence or a railway line laid across a migration route puts far more pasture out of reach than it physically _____ herders have opposed developments that look small on a map.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Lava cooling on the seafloor locks in the direction of the magnetic field at the moment it hardens. Cores drilled on either side of a mid-ocean ridge return matching sequences of reversed and normal _____ each of which can be tied to the same reversal recorded on the opposite side.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Chinese pharmacists sold ‘dragon bones’ as a remedy well into the nineteenth century, and the bones were ground up by the sackful. Scholars eventually recognised the marks scratched on them as an early form of Chinese _____ the bones turned out to be the divination records of a dynasty known until then only from much later accounts.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Timber laid up in layers set at right angles to one another behaves quite unlike a solid beam, and a panel of it will carry a floor load across a wide span. The material weighs about a fifth of what an equivalent concrete slab _____ a building framed in it can therefore stand on much lighter foundations.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The network reports every fifteen minutes, and a gap of more than an hour brings an engineer out to the site. Each of the twelve weather stations _____ its own battery and a small solar panel to keep the battery charged.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Two kilns fired the same clay on opposite sides of the valley, and their wares are told apart by the colour of the slip. The iron content measured in the sherds from the eastern kiln is nearly double _____ measured in the sherds from the western one.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Very little of the marsh survives in a condition anyone would call natural, and most of what does survive was cut for peat at some point. This fen is one of the few lowland sites in the county that _____ never been drained for agriculture.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Two atomic clocks of the same design, one at the foot of a tower and one at the top, no longer agree after a few days: the upper clock has run slightly fast. _____ a clock further from the mass of the Earth ticks at a faster rate than one closer to it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Simulating airflow on a computer costs a fraction of what a session in a wind tunnel costs, and the models have improved steadily for thirty years. _____ every new airliner wing is still tested on a physical model, because a simulation is only as good as its assumptions about turbulence.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Kente is woven in strips a hand's breadth wide, and the finished cloth is made by sewing the strips edge to edge so that their patterns line up. _____ the pattern of the whole cloth has to be worked out before the first strip goes on the loom, since a motif that spans two strips cannot be corrected afterwards.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise the condition on which the effect depends. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • At a country fair in 1906 Francis Galton collected 787 written guesses at the weight of an ox.
  • No individual guess was exactly right.
  • The middle value of the guesses fell within one pound of the true weight.
  • Galton had expected the crowd to do badly.
  • Later work finds the effect holds only when the guesses are made independently of one another.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Galton collected 787 guesses at the weight of an ox at a country fair in 1906.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The middle of 787 guesses came within a pound of the ox's true weight, and later work finds that the effect holds only where the guesses are made independently.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Galton had expected the crowd of fairgoers to do badly, and no individual guess was exactly right.

choices.label: D
choices.content: No single guess at the weight of the ox was exactly right, though the middle value was close.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how Cavendish's apparatus made the measurement possible. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Newton's law gives the force between two masses but not the value of the constant it contains.
  • In 1798 Henry Cavendish hung two small lead balls from the ends of a rod suspended on a wire.
  • Bringing two large lead spheres close to the small ones twisted the wire through a measurable angle.
  • The angle of twist gave the strength of the attraction between the balls.
  • Once the constant was known, the mass of the Earth could be calculated for the first time.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Once the constant had been measured, the mass of the Earth could be calculated.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Cavendish measured the tiny attraction between lead balls from the angle through which it twisted a suspended wire.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Newton's law gives the force between two masses but does not supply the constant it contains.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Cavendish carried out his experiment in 1798, more than a century after Newton.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise a limitation the language nests faced. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • In 1975 fewer than five per cent of Māori children in New Zealand could speak Māori.
  • The first kōhanga reo, or language nest, opened in 1982.
  • Preschoolers at a nest spend the day with fluent older speakers and hear only Māori.
  • By 1993 more than 800 nests were operating.
  • Children leaving the nests entered primary schools that taught in English.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The first language nest opened in 1982, and preschoolers there heard only Māori all day.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Fewer than five per cent of Māori children could speak the language in 1975.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Although more than 800 nests were operating by 1993, the children left them for primary schools that taught in English.

choices.label: D
choices.content: More than 800 language nests were operating by 1993.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A desert locust reared on its own is green, sluggish and solitary. Crowd it — brush the hind legs of enough individuals against one another — and within hours it starts to change colour, eat more and seek out others of its kind. The two forms were once described as separate species, so _____ is the change that crowding sets off.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Most minerals are reset by the heat of burial and re-melting. Zircon is not. A crystal that grew four billion years ago can pass through mountain-building, erosion and burial inside a sandstone and still hold the uranium clock sealed in it. What makes the mineral so useful to geologists is that it is so nearly _____.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “temper” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Clay dug from the riverbank cracks as it dries unless something coarse is worked into it first. The potters at this site used crushed shell, and the <u>temper</u> in a sherd is often the quickest way to tell one workshop's output from another's, since what was added was usually whatever lay nearest to hand.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Coarse material mixed into clay before it is fired.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The hardness given to steel by heating and cooling it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A moderating influence on a dispute.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The walls at Great Zimbabwe were laid without mortar, in courses of granite blocks split from the surrounding hills with fire and water. The finest of the coursing is so _____ that a blade cannot be pushed between two stones, and the walls have stood for six centuries with nothing binding them together.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The water under the Antarctic sea ice sits below the freezing point of ordinary blood. Notothenioid fish live in it because their blood carries proteins that fasten onto the first ice crystals to appear and stop them growing any further. The proteins do not warm the fish at all; they simply keep the crystals _____.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Analysts in 1943 mapped the bullet holes in aircraft returning from raids over Europe and proposed adding armour wherever the holes clustered. <u>Abraham Wald pointed out that the sample consisted entirely of aircraft that had come back.</u> Hits to the engines were rare in the data not because engines were seldom struck but because an aircraft struck there did not return to be examined. The armour went on the engines.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It describes the method by which the bullet holes were mapped.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It concedes that Wald's recommendation was never adopted.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It identifies the flaw in the reasoning that the rest of the text goes on to explain.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It supplies statistical support for the analysts' original proposal.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An alloy of nickel and titanium in roughly equal parts can be bent flat and will spring back to its original shape when it is warmed. <u>The metal has two crystal structures, and the change from one to the other is set off by temperature rather than by force.</u> Surgeons make use of this: a stent folded small enough to travel up an artery opens itself out at body heat, with no mechanism that could fail.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It gives the mechanism that accounts for the behaviour just described.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It raises a limitation of the alloy that the final sentence resolves.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It explains why nickel and titanium are combined in equal proportions.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It describes a surgical application of the alloy.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The skeleton of a Venus's flower basket is spun from silica at the temperature of the deep sea, with neither heat nor pressure to help. Its lattice of struts is braced diagonally at every corner, and the fibres themselves are laid down in layers of alternating thickness, so that a crack running through one layer is stopped at the next. Engineers who have modelled the structure find little in it that could be taken away without weakening the whole.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Silica is a stronger material than the alloys ordinarily used in engineering.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The sponge grows more slowly than other animals of comparable size.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Engineers have succeeded in manufacturing copies of the sponge's skeleton.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The sponge builds an efficiently braced, crack-resistant skeleton at ordinary deep-sea temperatures.

questions.stem: According to the text, why did vanilla grown outside Mexico fail to produce pods before 1841?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The vanilla orchid is pollinated in Mexico by insects that live nowhere else, so plants carried to other colonies flowered and set nothing. In 1841 Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old enslaved on Réunion, worked out that lifting the flap which separates the flower's male and female parts with a sliver of bamboo and pressing the two together does the job by hand. The method is still used, flower by flower, on the one morning each bloom is open.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Growers had not yet learned how to cure the pods properly.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The soils of the colonies were unsuited to the orchid.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The insects that pollinate the flower were not present.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The flowers opened for too short a time to be harvested.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferrari's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The geoglyphs on the Nazca plain are best seen from the air, which nobody could reach for centuries after they were made. Archaeologist Paulo Ferrari argues that the lines were meant to be walked in procession rather than viewed whole.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Each figure is drawn as a single continuous line that returns to its starting point, and the ground along the lines is compacted by heavy foot traffic.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Several of the largest figures are visible from hills at the edge of the plain.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The plain is one of the driest places on earth, which is why the lines have survived.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Some of the figures depict animals that do not live anywhere in the region.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Demir's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Elephants that reached Mediterranean islands in the Pleistocene evolved to a fraction of the size of their mainland ancestors. Palaeontologist Yusuf Demir argues that the driver was the limited food supply of a small island rather than the absence of large predators.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Dwarf elephants reached maturity at a younger age than mainland elephants did.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Mainland elephants of the same period were among the largest land mammals ever to live.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Across the islands studied, the degree of dwarfing tracks island area closely and shows no relation to whether large predators were present.

choices.label: D
choices.content: No fossils of large carnivores have been recovered from any of the islands.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Lodgepole pines in some stands hold their seed in cones sealed with resin that opens only in the heat of a fire; in other stands the cones open as they ripen. Ecologist Dawn Ferreira argues that the sealed form is favoured where fire sweeps through a stand at intervals shorter than the lifespan of a tree.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The proportion of trees bearing sealed cones is highest in the stands whose fire scars record the shortest intervals between burns.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Sealed cones keep seed viable for longer than cones that open as they ripen.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Lodgepole seedlings grow faster on ground cleared by fire than under a closed canopy.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Squirrels harvest cones of both kinds at similar rates.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A pendulum set swinging is acted on by gravity and by the tension in its wire, and neither force can turn the plane in which it swings. Yet the plane of a long pendulum hung in Paris is observed to rotate steadily through the day. Since nothing is turning the pendulum, what is actually rotating must be _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: the air through which the bob passes.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the wire from which the pendulum hangs.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the building and the ground beneath it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the bob about its own axis.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A neutrino crossing the Antarctic ice sheet very occasionally strikes a nucleus, and the collision throws off a faint flash of blue light. Detectors frozen into the ice reconstruct the neutrino's direction from the timing of that flash across a cubic kilometre of instruments. Because the light has to travel hundreds of metres before it reaches the nearest sensor, the array could not have been built in ice that was _____

choices.label: B
choices.content: colder than the bedrock beneath it.

choices.label: C
choices.content: younger than a few thousand years.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Merchants in the Baltic ports had more to fear from pirates and from local rulers than from one another. The Hanseatic League, an association of trading towns that at its height stretched from Novgorod to _____ its own warehouses, negotiated its own treaties and on occasion fought its own wars.

questions.passage: Cod caught off Newfoundland reached Mediterranean markets in good condition because the fish were split, salted and dried until they were as stiff as board. questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Carbon dioxide seeps into the deep water of some volcanic crater lakes and stays there, held down by the weight of the water above. If anything disturbs the layering — a landslide, a cold night, a heavy _____ the gas can come out of solution all at once and pour downhill as an invisible flood.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.passage: Sinan built more than three hundred structures for the Ottoman court and wrote almost nothing about any of them. Although the dome of the Selimiye mosque at Edirne is wider than the dome of Hagia _____ the architect mentions the achievement only in passing.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The tower has been fenced off since a stone fell from the parapet in 1974, and the bells have hung silent in the frame ever since. The trust's application for the repair grant ran to ninety pages and was refused twice before it succeeded. The money is to stabilise the roof, to rehang the bells and _____ the tower to visitors for the first time in half a century.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Dredging the harbour mouth was booked for a fortnight and ran into a second month. By the time the survey boat came back in June, the channel that silted up over the winter _____ to less than half its charted depth.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain what the shrimp's twelve receptors appear to be for. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Human eyes have three kinds of colour receptor.
  • A mantis shrimp's eyes have twelve.
  • Each of its eyes moves independently and judges distance on its own.
  • Tests show that mantis shrimp discriminate between similar colours less finely than humans do.
  • Researchers suggest the twelve receptors let the animal recognise a colour at once, without comparing signals.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Although a mantis shrimp has twelve kinds of colour receptor to a human's three, it discriminates similar colours less finely; the receptors appear to allow quick recognition rather than fine comparison.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Tests show that mantis shrimp discriminate between similar colours less finely than humans do.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A mantis shrimp has twelve kinds of colour receptor where a human has three.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Each of the shrimp's eyes moves independently and judges distance on its own.

  • Researchers laid oat flakes on a map of the Tokyo region where the suburban stations lie.
  • The mould first spread across the whole surface, then thinned its tubes back to the routes carrying the most flow.
  • The surviving network resembled the Tokyo rail network in total length and in resilience to a severed link.
  • The organism has no nervous system of any kind.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The surviving network resembled the Tokyo rail network in total length and in resilience to a severed link.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Physarum polycephalum is a single-celled organism that spreads as a network of tubes.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Researchers laid oat flakes on a map of the Tokyo region at the positions of the suburban stations.

choices.label: D
choices.content: By thinning its tubes back to the busiest routes, an organism with no nervous system produced a network resembling the Tokyo rail system in length and in resilience.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise why the written source is not sufficient on its own. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Landnámabók lists some four hundred settlers of Iceland and the land each of them claimed.
  • It was compiled roughly two centuries after the settlement it describes.
  • Pollen cores show birch woodland disappearing from the lowlands within a century of settlement.
  • The book says almost nothing about the clearance of woodland.
  • Archaeologists now use the two kinds of source together, checking one against the other.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Because the Landnámabók was compiled two centuries later and says almost nothing about woodland clearance, archaeologists check it against pollen cores showing the lowland birch disappearing within a century of settlement.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Pollen cores show birch woodland disappearing from the Icelandic lowlands within a century of settlement.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Archaeologists use written and environmental sources together, checking one against the other.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The Landnámabók lists some four hundred settlers and the land each of them claimed.

questions.passage: The churches at Lalibela were not built up from the ground. Masons began at the surface of a slab of red volcanic rock, cut a trench around the block they wanted, and then worked downwards and inwards, hollowing nave, aisles and windows out of a single mass of stone. questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

questions.passage: Finding longitude at sea means comparing local noon with the time at a known meridian, and that requires a clock that keeps time on a rolling deck through months of heat and damp. It came instead from a Yorkshire joiner whose fourth timekeeper lost a few seconds on the passage to Jamaica. The prize was paid only after a long argument and the intervention of the king.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

questions.passage: A naked mole-rat colony has one breeding female. The rest of the animals — several dozen, sometimes hundreds — dig, carry food and defend the tunnels without reproducing at all, and they will go on doing so for years. Suppress the queen's scent and several of the other females begin to develop ovaries within days. What holds the arrangement in place is therefore not anatomy but the queen's continuing presence.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Naked mole-rats are the only mammals known to live underground in large groups.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Non-breeding mole-rats stay that way because of the queen's presence, not because they are incapable of breeding.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A naked mole-rat colony collapses as soon as its queen dies.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Work in a mole-rat colony is divided among the animals according to their age.

questions.passage: The bronze weapons buried with the terracotta army came out of the ground bright. questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise the movement's eventual success despite the reception of the 1848 petition. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Chartists demanded a vote for every adult man and a secret ballot, among six points in all.
  • Their third petition was presented to Parliament in 1848.
  • The petition was said to carry nearly six million signatures.
  • A parliamentary committee counted fewer than two million and reported forgeries among them.
  • All but one of the six demands had become law within seventy years.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The third Chartist petition was presented to Parliament in 1848 and was said to carry nearly six million signatures.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A parliamentary committee counted fewer than two million signatures and reported forgeries among them.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The Chartists demanded a vote for every adult man and a secret ballot, among six points in all.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Although a parliamentary committee found the 1848 petition to carry far fewer signatures than had been claimed, all but one of the Chartists' six demands became law within seventy years.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain the effect of the new pigment on the prints that survive today. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Japanese woodblock printers used a blue made from dayflower petals that faded within a few years.
  • Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment, reached Japan through Dutch traders in the 1820s.
  • Prussian blue does not fade and can be printed in graded washes.
  • Hokusai's wave series of about 1831 uses it throughout.
  • Prints made from the 1830s onward keep their blues; earlier prints have usually lost theirs.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Japanese printers had used a blue made from dayflower petals, which faded within a few years.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Prussian blue reached Japan through Dutch traders in the 1820s and can be printed in graded washes.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Because Prussian blue does not fade as the dayflower blue did, prints made from the 1830s onward keep the blues that earlier prints have lost.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Hokusai's wave series of about 1831 uses Prussian blue throughout.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why the Taruga heads can be dated when most Nok heads cannot. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Nok terracotta heads were made in central Nigeria between about 900 BCE and 200 CE.
  • Many were found by tin miners washing gravel rather than by archaeologists.
  • A head washed out of gravel carries no record of the layer it came from.
  • Radiocarbon dating requires organic material found alongside the object.
  • Heads excavated in place at Taruga lay in a layer that also contained charcoal.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Because the Taruga heads were excavated in place, charcoal from the same layer could be used to date them, whereas heads washed out of gravel carry no such context.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Tin miners washing gravel found a great many Nok heads.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Radiocarbon dating requires organic material, and charcoal is organic material.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Nok terracotta heads were made in central Nigeria between about 900 BCE and 200 CE.

questions.stem: A landscaper spends \(6b+9\) minutes planting the beds and \(4b-2\) minutes planting the borders, where b is the number of beds. Which expression gives the total planting time, in minutes?

questions.stem: A quilt panel has an area of \(x^{2}+7x\) square centimetres. Which expression is equivalent to that area?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: Oranges are stacked so that the number of oranges in the nth layer of a stack is \(n^{2}+2\). How many oranges are in the 5th layer?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A pebble dropped from a bridge falls \(5t^{2}\) metres in the first t seconds of its fall. How many seconds does the pebble take to fall 45 metres?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A sluice gate releases water so that the flow speed, in centimetres per second, t seconds after the gate opens is \(u(t)=\frac{120}{t+2}\). What is the flow speed 4 seconds after the gate opens?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A crystallographer records a count as \(\left(a^{4}\right)^{3}\), where \(a>1\). Which expression is equivalent to that count?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A rumour spreads through a village so that the number of people who have heard it h hours after it starts is \(P(h)=5\cdot 2^{h}\). How many people have heard the rumour 4 hours after it starts?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A trail mix is made with 2 parts almonds to 3 parts raisins by mass. One batch contains 480 grams of raisins. How many grams of almonds are in that batch?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The membership of a museum rose from 400 people to 460 people in one year. By what percent did the membership rise?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem:
The table gives the number of minutes a swimmer trained on each of four days.
DayMinutes trained
Monday48
Tuesday65
Wednesday52
Thursday61
How many more minutes did the swimmer train on Tuesday than on Monday?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A hockey team scored 1, 3, 3, 4 and 9 goals in its five matches this month. What is the mean number of goals the team scored per match?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A surveyor stakes out a triangular plot in which two of the angles measure 48° and 79°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the third angle?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A gardener marks out a flowerbed shaped like a triangle whose base measures 14 metres and whose height measures 6 metres. How many square metres of ground does the flowerbed cover?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A storage bin is a cube whose edges are each 7 feet long. What is the volume of the bin, in cubic feet?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A ladder 26 feet long leans against a vertical wall, with the foot of the ladder 10 feet from the base of the wall. How many feet up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A shipping planner writes two loading constraints as \(4x+3y=26\) and \(kx+9y=57\), where x and y are the numbers of two kinds of container and k is a constant. No pair \((x,y)\) satisfies both constraints. What is the value of k?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A pyrometer converts a raw count x into a temperature offset \(f(x)\), and f is a linear function. The instrument's calibration certificate records \(f(2)=-5\) and \(f(8)=13\). What is the value of \(f(-3)\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A community kitchen makes soup and stew. Each litre of soup needs 2 minutes of preparation and each litre of stew needs 5 minutes, and the kitchen has at most 240 minutes of preparation time. The kitchen must also make at least twice as many litres of soup as of stew. What is the greatest whole number of litres of stew the kitchen can make?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A rectangular reflecting pool measuring 12 metres by 8 metres is bordered on all four sides by a walkway of uniform width w metres. The walkway covers exactly as much ground as the pool itself. What is the value of w?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: Two stages of a water treatment plant are modelled by \(g(x)=2x-5\) and \(f(x)=x^{2}+x\), applied in that order so that the output of g becomes the input of f. Which expression is equivalent to \(f(g(x))\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A ballistics report gives the height of a test round above a datum line, in metres, as \(h(x)=2x^{2}-16x+35\). Which form of the expression displays the least height the round reaches as a constant or coefficient?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: Two pumps working together empty a flooded cellar in 4 hours. Working alone, the larger pump would take 6 hours less than the smaller pump would take alone. How many hours would the smaller pump take to empty the cellar alone?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A materials engineer reduces the quantity \(\frac{\left(8a^{9}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}{2a^{3}}\), where \(a>0\). Which expression is equivalent to that quantity?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The cross-section of a skateboard bowl is the graph of \(y=a(x-3)^{2}-8\), where a is a constant and x and y are measured in feet. The lowest point of the bowl is at \((3,-8)\), and the rim of the bowl passes through \((5,4)\). What is the value of a?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A control loop is described as critically damped when the equation \(3x^{2}+kx+12=0\) has exactly one real solution, where k is a positive constant. What is the value of k?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A pharmacist mixes a 15% saline solution with a 40% saline solution to obtain 500 millilitres of a 24% saline solution. How many millilitres of the 40% solution does the pharmacist use?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A forester selected 200 oaks at random from a plantation of 4,000 oaks and found that 38 of the selected oaks showed signs of a fungal blight. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
questions.subject: MATH

choices.label: A
choices.content: Exactly 760 of the oaks in the plantation show signs of the blight.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The blight will eventually reach every oak in the plantation.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Nothing about the plantation as a whole can be concluded from a sample.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It is reasonable to estimate that about 760 of the oaks in the plantation show signs of the blight.

questions.stem: A shop recorded the number of umbrellas it sold on each of 9 days, and the mean of the 9 figures was 14. The owner then found that one day's figure had been entered as 8 when it should have been 26. What is the mean of the 9 corrected figures?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A dye vat must be filled with 3,600 litres of liquid in which the ratio of water to concentrate is 11 to 1 by volume. Concentrate is sold only in 25-litre drums. What is the least number of drums of concentrate needed to fill the vat?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem:

SeasonVisitorsMean spend per visitor ($)
Spring8,4006.50
Summer15,2009.25
Autumn7,6005.80
Winter4,3004.20
By how many dollars did total summer spending exceed the combined total spending of the other three seasons?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A steel truss plate has the shape of a right triangle. The perpendicular dropped from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse divides the hypotenuse into two segments, of lengths 4 centimetres and 9 centimetres. What is the length, in centimetres, of that perpendicular?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A conical funnel has a radius of 6 centimetres and a height of 16 centimetres, with its apex at the bottom. Sand fills the funnel to half its height, measured upward from the apex. What volume of sand, in cubic centimetres, is in the funnel?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A surveyor's plot is a right triangle \(ABC\) with the right angle at C, and the surveyor's notes record \(\tan A=\frac{5}{12}\). What is the value of \(\sin A\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A workshop makes brackets on two machines. Machine P makes 4 brackets an hour and machine Q makes 7 brackets an hour. Machine Q may be run for at most 8 hours, and the workshop needs at least 88 brackets. What is the least whole number of hours for which machine P must be run?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The price of a ski resort's season pass is a linear function of the number of lifts the pass covers. A pass covering 6 lifts costs $342, and a pass covering 10 lifts costs $510. How many dollars does a pass covering 15 lifts cost?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: In a two-person relay, the first runner covers a certain distance at a constant 12 kilometres per hour, and the second runner covers twice that distance at a constant 8 kilometres per hour. The relay takes 4 hours in total. How many kilometres did the first runner cover?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A solid sphere of radius 6 centimetres is melted down and recast, with no loss of metal, into identical solid cylinders each of radius 2 centimetres and height 3 centimetres. How many such cylinders are made?
questions.subject: MATH
